newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: INTERVIEW-ANZ Grindlays hopes to get more mandates.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-ANZ Grindlays hopes to get more mandates.

text.p: ANZ Grindlays Bank said it hoped to get more mandates for sovereign issues after successful flotation of a three-year $300 million floating rate Eurobond for Pakistan.

"I know the government is asking for tenders for various types of transactions and for advice and for new innovative products and we will be bidding for the business," ANZ Gridlays general manager in Pakistan, Azhar Hamid, told Reuters.

He said the Pakistani government had been encouraged after Grindlays successfully closed the $300 million issue at 398 basis points above London interbank offer rate (LIBOR) in May, which was three times larger than originally planned.
Newspapers said the government had short-listed nine firms to lead the raising of $500 million against securitisation of expatriate workers' remittances.
Hamid said in the interview on Tuesday his bank did not bid for the particular issue but was in the run for other products.
He said the government had plans to float more paper in international markets in major currencies "to replace short-term funding with reasonably medium-term debt."
"The bond is currently quoted at a slight premium that means that from May 31 to now market perception has slightly improved, which is a good sign for the country.
"I would be surprised if the government does not come back to us or to any other bank to try and raise further funds because they have to balance their position," he said.
"In addition to that we hope that privatisation proceeds over the next three to four years' period will enable the government to get rid of the expensive portion of the foreign debt," he said.
Pakistan's foreign debt is estimated at around $29 billion.

"We have tested the waters and the market has responded favourably," he said, adding that international credit-rating agencies would review Pakistan's rating favourably if the International Monetary Fund restored its lending programme.
"Once that happens we can hopefully look at a figure of $1.5 billion to $2 billion coming through FDI (foreign direct investment)," he said.
An IMF mission was due to arrive on Wednesday to start negotiations for a new medium-term loan to support the government's structural reforms.

"I personally feel confident that IMF lending will be restored based on the government's economic policies which are right, progressive and provide the incentives for more industrialisation," he said.
Hamid said his bank was very optimistic about Pakistan, especially in view of the policies adopted by Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif.

"If the government policies work the way we think they should, I would reckon the reasonable rate for five-year paper for Pakistan risk should not be more than two to 2.5 percent over LIBOR," he said. "But at the moment the government is raising one-year money at 1.9 percent which, given the risk which is pretty high, is a good rate."
